analysis.one_liner: Keeps Social Security checks flowing if trust funds run dry, paid for by taxing the ultra-wealthy and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: If Social Security's trust funds ever ran out of money, this bill would automatically send general tax revenue into them each month so benefits keep being paid in full. It would also fast-track a solvency bill through both chambers with limited debate and no amendments, and require that any new funding come only from the ultra-wealthy and corporations — not from benefit cuts or taxes on most people. It would additionally require a Social Security field office in every county with more than 150,000 residents.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 67 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits, including more than 9 million veterans and over 6 million children, would be guaranteed full payments even if the trust funds become insolvent [S2]. People who need in-person help — those who cannot use the phone or internet — would gain guaranteed access to a local field office if their county has more than 150,000 residents [S2]. The cost would fall on ultra-wealthy households and corporations through new taxes [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and their families

how_it_helps.text: Whenever the Commissioner of Social Security certifies that the Old-Age and Survivors or Disability trust fund cannot finance benefit payments, the bill requires a monthly general-tax appropriation equal to whatever is needed to keep paying benefits in full [S2].

Under the bill, any solvency bill triggered by insolvency must keep full benefits, must not cut benefits or raise taxes on anyone but the ultra-wealthy and corporations, and would move to a floor vote within 15 days in the House, with committees discharged after 5 days if they fail to act [S2].
In the Senate, the solvency bill could not be filibustered: debate is capped at 10 hours, all amendments and points of order are barred, and the vote must follow immediately [S2].

The bill requires the Social Security Administration to operate a field office in every county with a population above 150,000, citing seniors, veterans, and children who rely on in-person access [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ultra-wealthy households and corporations, who would bear any additional funding need through new taxes if the fast-track solvency mechanism were triggered, and federal general-revenue taxpayers, since the automatic trust-fund bailout would be drawn from income-tax money rather than payroll taxes [S2].

drawbacks.text: The automatic monthly appropriation to an insolvent trust fund would come from general tax revenue, adding to federal deficits or competing with other spending, with no offset or limit specified in the bill [S2].

The fast-track procedure strips committees of real review, bars every amendment, and locks in one specific funding approach — taxing only the ultra-wealthy and corporations — regardless of what a future Congress might judge best when insolvency actually arrives [S2].

The bill is partly a political statement: its findings name former President Trump, Speaker Mike Johnson, J.D. Vance, and Rick Scott as threats to Social Security and cite a Republican Study Committee plan to raise the retirement age to 69, which makes it more of a messaging vehicle than a negotiation starting point [S2].
The field-office mandate covers roughly every county above 150,000 people but includes no funding estimate, staffing plan, or cost ceiling [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — guaranteeing full Social Security payments during insolvency and requiring the cost to fall on the wealthy and corporations rather than on beneficiaries — is substantial for tens of millions of people. The costs are real but ordinary for a guarantee of this size: general-revenue transfers would add pressure on the deficit, and the no-amendment fast-track trades legislative flexibility for certainty. The bill's partisan findings and lack of any cosponsor, however, made it primarily a statement of priorities rather than a viable negotiated fix to Social Security's long-term financing gap.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pat Ryan introduced the bill on August 9, 2024, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, for procedural provisions, the Rules Committee [S1][S4].
On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security — a step that typically means a committee has no plan to act on the full bill soon [S4].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House [S3].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ultra-wealthy households and corporations are better off, because the mechanism that would have required them to bear the cost of shoring up Social Security never advanced. House leaders and the Ways and Means chairman also kept the option off the floor without having to vote against it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy households, corporations, and House leaders

for.name: Rep. Patrick Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleagues joined as cosponsors

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat in his committee and was sent to a subcommittee in December

against.name: Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the bill criticized him by name in its findings

sides.party_line_note: There were no recorded votes; the bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and its findings targeted named Republican leaders, so it never reached a point where party positions were tested.

industries.note: If the fast-track were triggered, any funding needed to keep Social Security paying full benefits must be borne by the ultra-wealthy through new taxes [S2]. Because the bill died, that obligation never materialized.
The bill's solvency mechanism names corporations alongside the ultra-wealthy as the only permitted source of additional funds [S2]. The bill's failure leaves them with no new tax burden.
The automatic monthly transfers into an insolvent trust fund would be drawn from general tax revenue, spreading some cost across all federal taxpayers rather than only payroll-tax contributors [S2].
